title: Trump DOJ unlawfully fired Epstein prosecutor Maurene Comey, judge rules
description: Daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, Maurene Comey, leaves the Albert V. Bryan United States Courthouse on Nov. 13, 2025 in Alexandria, Virgin
body: Daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, Maurene Comey, leaves the Albert V. Bryan United States Courthouse on Nov. 13, 2025 in Alexandria, Virginia. Alex Wong | Getty ImagesA federal judge ruled Monday that the Department of Justice's firing of New York federal prosecutor Maurene Comey last year was unlawful.Judge Jesse Furman ordered that Comey, who is the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, be retroactively reinstated to her job as an assistant United States attorney in the Southern District of New York. The judge also ordered that she receive back pay from July 16 through December 20, 2025, when he inferred that Comey accepted another job, in the ruling in U.S. District Court in Manhattan.Maurene Comey, who had been involved with prosecutions of Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice, Ghislaine Maxwell, and Sean "Diddy" Combs, was fired in July 2025. She later sued the Department of Justice, challenging its right to terminate her.Her father has long been a target of criticism from President Donald Trump. James Comey, whom Trump fired as FBI director in 2017,  is being prosecuted for allegedly threatening Trump's life by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells forming the number "86 47." His attorneys are seeking to have that case tossed out.Furman, in his ruling for Maurene Comey in U.S. District Court in Manhattan, rejected the DOJ's arguments that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi could remove a federal prosecutor "at will" and without cause, and that current AG Todd Blanche could ratify that act after the fact.Furman also rejected the DOJ's argument that even if the Civil Service Reform Act requires removal of a prosecutor for cause, an attorney general's firing of her constituted an implicit determination that she was removed "for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service.""The Court need not dwell long on Defendants' second statutory argument justifyingComey's removal," Furman said, referring to that claim. "That is because the argument borders on frivolous."The judge said the DOJ all but admitted that its argument that the attorney general had power to fire Comey under Article II of the Constitution sought "to overturn nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent.""This Court, however, is bound to follow the Supreme Court's precedents unless and until the Supreme Court overturns them," Furman wrote.Comey's lawyers, in a statement Monday, said, "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms. Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law.""As the Court correctly held, to accept the government's argument about unlimited executive power 'would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation's constitutional system,'" the lawyers said. "This decision reaffirms our bedrock system of checks and balances: the President is not above the law."The DOJ, in a statement, said, "The Department disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course."That appeal would happen after Furman issues a final judgment in the case. The judge did not rule on a claim by Comey that her First Amendment rights were violated by her firing, and gave her until Nov. 9 to file arguments on why that claim should not be dismissed as moot given his order in her favor on other grounds. CNBC has requested comment on the ruling from the White House. Comey, in a note to colleagues at the U.S. Attorney's Office after she was fired, wrote, "If a career prosecutor can be fired without reason, fear may seep into the decisions of those who remain.""Fear is the tool of a tyrant, wielded to suppress independent thought. Instead of fear, let this moment fuel the fire that already burns in the heart of this place," she wrote. "A fire of righteous indignation at abuses of power. Of commitment to seek justice for victims."

schema.headline: Trump DOJ unlawfully fired Epstein prosecutor Maurene Comey, judge rules

title: Mortgage rates above 7% are the 'new normal'—here's why
description: Everyone seems to agree that mortgage rates above 7% are the new "normal."The phrase keeps popping up lately in public comments from housing economist
body: Everyone seems to agree that mortgage rates above 7% are the new "normal."The phrase keeps popping up lately in public comments from housing economists, including Lawrence Yun, chief economist for the National Association of Realtors, and Robert Dietz, chief economist for the National Association of Home Builders. It's a sentiment increasingly reflected in forecasts, too, with major housing groups predicting mortgage rates will remain above 7% well into 2027. Fannie Mae forecasts mortgage rates could average 7.5% in 2027, while the Mortgage Bankers Association expects them to remain above 7%. That means the 3% or 4% mortgage rates borrowers were used to in the years before 2022 are unlikely to return anytime soon. "We could definitely see some movement up and down depending on data, but we're just not in the same economic environment we were in during the 2010s or the pandemic," says Jenna Stauffer, a broker and market analyst with Sotheby's International Realty.Why mortgage rates could stay higher for longerMortgage rates tend to move with the 10-year Treasury yield, which serves as a benchmark because mortgages are typically paid off or refinanced well before their 30-year term. And there are reasons to think those longer-term borrowing costs could remain elevated.One is persistently high inflation. When inflation remains elevated, investors generally demand higher yields on long-term bonds to compensate for the declining purchasing power of the money they'll eventually be repaid. Inflation, as measured by the Fed's preferred PCE price index, hasn't been below the central bank's 2% target since February 2021.But inflation isn't the only factor. The federal government is borrowing heavily, while the artificial intelligence boom is fueling enormous private investment in data centers, power generation and other infrastructure, says Selma Hepp, chief economist at real estate data firm Cotality. Together, that increased demand for capital can put upward pressure on longer-term borrowing costs, she says.Compared to the 2010s, "we've moved from a world with more capital than investment opportunities to one with tremendous competition for capital," Hepp says. Low inflation, abundant savings and relatively weak demand for capital helped keep mortgage rates low during that period, she says.Demand for mortgage bonds has weakened, too, putting upward pressure on mortgage rates. Banks have become more reluctant to hold mortgage-backed securities since the 2022-23 rate spike produced steep losses on bond portfolios, says Tom Graff, chief investment officer at wealth management firm Facet.  That's because bond prices generally fall when interest rates rise. The failures of Silicon Valley Bank and First Republic also prompted greater regulatory scrutiny of banks' bond holdings, he says.During the pandemic, the Fed pushed rates in the opposite direction. The Federal Reserve bought large quantities of Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities to push longer-term borrowing costs lower, helping drive mortgage rates to historic lows. The Fed has since stepped away from actively buying mortgage-backed securities, says Steve Kaminski, head of residential lending at TD Bank.With those low-rate conditions no longer in place, "mortgage rates will likely remain elevated for at least the next year," Kaminski says.What would it take for mortgage rates to fall?Getting mortgage rates back to around 6% would likely require lower inflation, slower economic growth or less pressure from government borrowing to help bring down the 10-year Treasury yield, Hepp says.Kaminski similarly says getting below 7% would require lower inflation and lower Treasury yields. A weakening economy could also push rates lower as investors seek the relative safety of Treasury bonds, lowering their yields, he says.Whether that happens is uncertain, which is why Hepp says she doesn't like calling 7% the "new normal," since there's nothing permanent about that particular number. But the low inflation, abundant capital and accommodative Fed policies that helped produce 3% and 4% mortgages are no longer in place, she says.For would-be homebuyers, that means waiting for significantly lower mortgage rates could be a gamble. "I don't think we should expect to return to the financial conditions that routinely produced 3% and 4% mortgages," Hepp says.

schema.headline: Mortgage rates above 7% are the 'new normal'—here's why

title: NBA enters prediction markets with Kalshi, Polymarket partnerships
description: Tari Eason #17, Amen Thompson #1 of the Houston Rockets and Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers go up for the rebound during the game during R
body: Tari Eason #17, Amen Thompson #1 of the Houston Rockets and Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers go up for the rebound during the game during Round One Game Five of the 2026 NBA Playoffs on April 29, 2026 at Crypto.Com Arena in Los Angeles, California. Adam Pantozzi | National Basketball Association | Getty ImagesThe NBA is embracing prediction markets for the first time by naming leading platforms Kalshi and Polymarket as its preferred exchanges. Through the agreements, the league said there will be "significant integrity" protections for NBA markets, including limitations on which types of event contracts can be featured and information-sharing requirements regarding suspicious trades. "Protecting the integrity of the game is our top priority," said Scott Kaufman-Ross, NBA head of media distribution and partnerships in a press release. "These partnerships represent an important step in establishing a framework that creates new opportunities to engage our fans."As part of the announcements, the league also signed a memorandum of understanding with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that asserts prediction markets are under its purview. The agreement seeks to maintain the integrity of both the NBA and event contract markets, the memo said, through exchanges of information. The NBA is the latest league to create partnerships with the booming prediction markets industry, which has seen much of its growth over the past year come from the popularity of its sports-related offerings. The NHL in October 2025 announced partnerships with both Kalshi and Polymarket, while the MLB announced a relationship with the latter company in March. Those same contracts, though, are under fire by states across the country, who argue that the offerings amount to sports betting and should be regulated by them. Platforms and the CFTC argue that event contracts are swaps, a type of derivative, and thus are regulated at the federal level. Courts across the country have delivered conflicting rulings on the issue, and many expect the Supreme Court will likely be needed to resolve the dispute. "The NBA is one of the most influential sports leagues in the world, and we're excited to work together to bring fans closer to the game," said Ari Borod, president of sports business development at Polymarket, in the press release.  As preferred exchanges, Kalshi and Polymarket get rights to use NBA intellectual property along with marketing and licensing rights. watch now"It's an exciting time for both NBA fans and Kalshi users," Adam Barrick, head of sports partnerships at Kalshi, said in the release. "The relationship we've built together reflects a shared mindset that prioritizes fan engagement, innovation and safety."The NBA's move on Monday now leaves the NFL as the outlier among major American sports leagues when it comes to prediction markets. Earlier this month, the NFL in an amicus brief to the Supreme Court said that sports-related event contracts should be regulated by the states rather than the CFTC. The league added that it's not opposed to the markets, but rather thinks they should have more guardrails.At the time, Kalshi told CNBC it had tried to work more closely with the NFL, but that the league hadn't engaged. Adam Silver, the commissioner of the NBA, though, took a different approach on the regulation question in an interview with CNBC's Contessa Brewer in early October. "From at least the NBA standpoint, we have roughly 40 different jurisdictions regulating us right now," he said. "So to have a consistent policy nationally, I think would be in our best interest."— CNBC's Jessica Golden contributed reportingDisclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: NBA enters prediction markets with Kalshi, Polymarket partnerships

title: Ukraine disputes Elon Musk’s claim that its military violated Starlink terms during drone operations
description: Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal at a combat positio
body: Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal at a combat position in the Donetsk region, Ukraine, on Oct. 16, 2026.Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesA Ukrainian official disputed SpaceX CEO Elon Musk's claim that Ukraine's military violated Starlink's terms of service, prompting the company to restrict Ukraine's access to the high-speed satellite technology.Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote an online post on Sunday contesting Musk's reason for temporarily throttling Ukraine's access to high-speed service from SpaceX's Starlink satellite communication systems. Ukrainian officials previously said the restrictions disrupted the country's military drone services and left the country vulnerable to Russian attacks.Musk on Saturday claimed in a post on X that the "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people."Beskrestnov pushed back on Musk's allegation, arguing that pre-existing restrictions on the systems would have made it "physically impossible" for Ukraine to use Starlink in the types of strikes the SpaceX CEO described."It is very strange that Elon Musk is unaware of the operational limitations of Starlink in Ukraine," Beskrestnov wrote in a post on Telegram, noting that Starlink's civilian system in Ukraine "does not function over the territory of Russia" and that Ukrainian drones operating with Starlink have had a speed restriction of 70 to 90 km/h (roughly 43 to 56 miles per hour) for months."Consequently, it is PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE for us to use commercial Starlink for deep-strike or medium-range strike operations," Beskrestnov wrote.Ukraine officials acknowledged on Saturday that high-speed service for SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield satellite communications systems had been restored. The country has blamed that restricted service for disrupting its drone air defense capabilities during frequent Russian air attacks.Starshield is SpaceX's military-focused satellite network for government and national security use, built on technology developed for Starlink, the company's broader commercial satellite internet network.Before Musk acknowledged that he had restricted the systems, confusion and speculation abounded over who ordered the high-speed service changes.At one point, Musk wrote in a social media post that the U.S. government was behind the decision, though President Donald Trump claimed he had no knowledge of the decision. Ukrainian officials have also said Starlink or the U.S. had imposed the restrictions without warning, leaving the country blindsided. Musk has not explained the reported lack of notification to Ukraine before his company implemented the restrictions.Musk and SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment.The restrictions on Starlink and Starshield in war-torn Ukraine have driven Ukraine and its allies to seek or build alternative, "sovereign" satellite communication systems. Poland's Deputy Minister of National Defense, Cezary Tomczyk, discussed his country's plans on a podcast called Influence Zone (Strefa Influenceów) earlier this month. Ukraine also announced partnerships with Norway and Finland's mobile giant Nokia, as well as satellite maker ICEYE, to develop alternatives.Beyond Ukraine, several countries are also exploring sovereign systems. The European Union is building IRIS², a constellation of hundreds of satellites, but it doesn't expect its first launches until 2029.SpaceX's Starlink generated $5.25 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up from $3.1 billion a year earlier. Revenue from consumer Starlink subscribers totaled $3.12 billion, while the company generated $2.13 billion from government and enterprise customers during the quarter.A wide array of customers, including non-government entities, the governments of Poland and France, and the Pentagon, have paid SpaceX to provide its Starlink and Starshield hardware and wireless internet services to Ukraine.

schema.headline: Ukraine disputes Elon Musk’s claim that its military violated Starlink terms during drone operations

title: Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer
description: The Amgen logo is displayed outside Amgen headquarters in Thousand Oaks, California, on May 17, 2023.Mario Tama | Getty ImagesA drug from Amgen could
body: The Amgen logo is displayed outside Amgen headquarters in Thousand Oaks, California, on May 17, 2023.Mario Tama | Getty ImagesA drug from Amgen could give patients with a notoriously aggressive form of lung cancer significantly more time to live when added to an immunotherapy from AstraZeneca, a study found.Full results from a late-stage trial released Saturday show that adding Amgen's immunotherapy Imdelltra to AstraZeneca's Imfinzi drug slashed the risk of death by 58% in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, a fast-growing disease that has spread beyond the lung where it began.The drug combination extended their median overall survival to 21.1 months compared with 12.7 months with AstraZeneca's drug alone, the trial found.That means half of patients in the group that took the combination regimen were alive for at least roughly 21 months. The trial tested the combo as a maintenance therapy in patients who received initial treatment with Imfinzi and chemotherapy, and whose cancer had not progressed."I think there are moments in medicine when you see a piece of data that is so profound that it's going to transform the standard of care for patients, and I think, honestly, we're at that moment," said Dr. Paul Burton, Amgen's chief medical officer, in an interview.The combination "has the potential to take on one of the most aggressive cancers that we deal with today, and almost convert it into a chronic disease," he said, adding that "these data say that's a possibility." The results also suggest a greater commercial opportunity for Imdelltra, which posted $288 million in sales during the second quarter, up 115% year over year. The drug already generated $627 million in global sales in 2025 and appears to be on its way to becoming a blockbuster medicine, or hitting the $1 billion sales threshold.Small cell lung cancer remains difficult to treat because, even if chemotherapy initially works well for most patients, the disease often returns or progresses within months, said lead trial investigator Dr. Jacob Sands, who is the associate chief of the Lowe Center for Thoracic Oncology at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. He said immunotherapy has helped a small subset of patients achieve years of disease control, but most have not experienced similarly durable benefits, highlighting the need for better treatments. There are roughly 31,000 new small cell lung cancer cases in the U.S. each year, and an estimated 60% to 70% of those people are diagnosed with extensive-stage disease.Sands said the benefits in the trial were seen across subgroups of patients, including those whose cancer spread to the brain or liver. Disease that has spread to those organs is associated with poorer treatment outcomes.He added that with longer-term follow-up data on the patients, the 21-month figure "may evolve further and hopefully will substantially improve," similar to what Amgen saw in a Phase 1 trial on the immunotherapy combination. In that early-stage trial on a smaller number of patients, a long-term follow-up showed the benefit was sustained for years. Using Imdelltra earlier Amgen said the findings also suggest that using Imdelltra earlier in a patient's treatment could meaningfully alter the trajectory of the disease. Imdelltra is currently approved for patients whose small cell lung cancer has progressed while they are on, or after, platinum-based chemotherapy.Researchers specifically tested whether adding Imdelltra could help patients live longer than continuing Imfinzi alone, which is already approved as a first treatment for this type of lung cancer. Amgen said nearly 80% of patients who started taking both drugs were alive at one year compared with 53% receiving Imfinzi alone. Imdelltra's "big impact" on controlling the disease and ultimately how long people live highlights the importance of including it in first-line maintenance treatment, Sands said. That refers to ongoing therapy given after an initial heavy treatment, such as chemotherapy or surgery.Burton added that it positions Amgen's drug to be an "indispensable backbone therapy" for small cell lung cancer, regardless of the other immunotherapy that can be paired with it. Imdelltra binds to DLL3, a protein on cancer cells, and CD3, a protein on T cells, which are a type of immune cell that can kill cancer. By binding to both, Imdelltra brings T cells into close contact with tumor cells, helping the immune system destroy the cancer. Imfinzi, made by AstraZeneca, is an immunotherapy that blocks a protein called PD-L1, which cancer cells use to evade the immune system. The drugs work together in complementary ways: Imfinzi helps remove the brakes on the immune response, while Imdelltra brings T cells directly to cancer cells and helps activate them to attack the tumor.The study, which was presented at a major cancer meeting called the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress, did not test whether the combination was better than other first-line treatment approaches. Still, the findings suggest Amgen's drug could be another option offered to small cell lung cancer patients earlier in their treatment. Kate Brenan, a 44-year-old mother of two from Denver, sees that as a win on its own. She was diagnosed with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer in early January 2024. Brenan underwent six rounds of a common combination chemotherapy, followed by chest radiation and later whole-brain radiation after the cancer spread. In September 2024, she started Imdelltra and has had no evidence of disease ever since. "I think that it's remarkable how quickly things are changing in the world of small cancer treatment options," Brenan told CNBC, adding that Imdelltra potentially becoming an earlier treatment option "can only be a good thing for the patients moving forward, and I'm really excited about that."

schema.headline: Amgen says drug combo cuts risk of death by 58% in patients with aggressive lung cancer

title: Can GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a moderate who's bucked Trump, keep his Pennsylvania swing seat?
description: Over nearly 10 years in Congress, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick has cultivated an image as a middle-of-the-road GOP lawmaker who operates above the partisan
body: Over nearly 10 years in Congress, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick has cultivated an image as a middle-of-the-road GOP lawmaker who operates above the partisan fray and is willing to buck President Donald Trump.It's a formula that has allowed Fitzpatrick, who is among the most moderate lawmakers on Capitol Hill according to his hometown newspaper, to win swing voters and consistently outperform his party in a highly competitive district that opted for Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris in 2024. But in a year when Republican candidates across the country are being weighed down by Trump, Fitzpatrick is facing a stiff challenge from Democrat Bob Harvie in Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District, and testing whether his personal brand can carry him in a difficult national political environment."Brian Fitzpatrick is Brian Fitzpatrick. I'm not Donald Trump. I'm not anybody else. And that's the way voters should approach this," Fitzpatrick told CNBC. "I'm not happy with [Trump]. I'm not happy with his tone. I don't think he's done a sufficient job. I think leaders are supposed to unite our country, unify people. He has not done that."The battle between Fitzpatrick and Harvie comes as Trump's approval rating craters, the Iran war drags on and consumer prices rise. The contest is one of the approximately four dozen House seats considered in play in the Nov. 3 election that will decide control of Congress for the last two years of Trump's term. Pennsylvania voters are often an indicator of how the country will swing overall, and because the state is on the East Coast, Fitzpatrick's district is one to watch as returns come in.Democrats are on offense and spending money in districts previously thought out of reach — including Fitzpatrick's, in a race that could signal Democratic success outside of just the most vulnerable seats.But Harvie, a former high school social studies teacher and county commissioner, is still a long shot to win. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted the race in Democrats' direction, from "Likely R" to "Lean R," earlier this month. Erin Covey, who leads coverage of House races at the Cook Report, called Fitzpatrick Democrats' "white whale."As part of Democrats' final push to unseat Fitzpatrick, Harvie was joined earlier this month by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro for a rally in Bucks County."This is an incredibly important state," Jeffries told reporters after the rally. "The commonwealth is a big swing state, and Bucks County is a big swing county. And so this is a critically important race."Fitzpatrick grew up in Bucks County, which makes up much of the district, and is a former FBI agent who succeeded his brother, Michael, in 2017. He's a co-chair of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus and, according to a recent Philadelphia Inquirer analysis of his voting record, has voted against the White House and his party this Congress more than any other House Republican. The paper endorsed Harvie earlier this month.Fitzpatrick is also part of a bipartisan group that's been outspoken as the White House has taken a more conciliatory tone toward Russia in recent weeks. He led a bill last week that would undo Trump's recent authorization of the U.S. purchase of Russian diesel. And he signed a bipartisan letter urging the Department of Defense to restore Ukraine's access to satellite communications that are critical to the country's defenses, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the services were downgraded. Fitzpatrick threatened to pursue the firing of U.S. officials responsible for the slowdown, The New York Times reported.Fitzpatrick is seeking his sixth House term and for much of his career has easily warded off Democratic challenges. Christopher Nicholas, a Republican consultant based in Pennsylvania, said Fitzpatrick "has been the most moderate member of the House.""If they are able to beat him this cycle, it is definitely going to be a great night for Democrats," Covey said. Harvie casts Fitzpatrick as a rubber stamp for Trump and questions the claims of bipartisanship. While Fitzpatrick was one of only two Republicans to vote against the final version of Republicans' 2025 signature tax and spending package, he voted in favor of an earlier iteration in the House that sent the measure to the Senate and set it on a path to passage. Fitzpatrick has said he supported the initial draft of the bill, but opposed cuts to Medicaid that were added in the Senate.Harvie also called out Fitzpatrick's mixed record on tariffs. Fitzpatrick voted to overturn Trump's tariffs on Canada, but has also sided with most Republicans on procedural votes to limit Congress' ability to challenge some of the president's tariffs. Fitzpatrick voted in favor of a controversial, Trump-backed election bill, dubbed the SAVE America Act, which would require identification to cast a ballot and proof of citizenship to register to vote. And he backed a controversial GOP immigration proposal and Trump's bid to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America.""When it comes to our economics in this country, people are suffering," Harvie, a Bucks County native, told CNBC. "The government is one that is totally detached from the people it's supposed to serve. Internationally, we've never been weaker and more isolated … and all of that is because of Donald Trump and because of people like Brian Fitzpatrick, who are just letting him run amok."Fitzpatrick is still favored to win. But Brit Crampsie, a Democratic strategist based in Pennsylvania, said Democrats have a stronger candidate in Harvie than they have in past cycles. "Bob Harvie, from his time as a school teacher to a local official, has deep ties to this community, and he's very representative of this community," Crampsie said. "He understands Bucks County and has high name ID."In addition to Trump's low favorability and voters' economic concerns, Fitzpatrick and other Pennsylvania Republicans must also contend with one of the most popular governors in the country at the top of the ticket. Shapiro is expected to win reelection easily, according to recent polling. In Fitzpatrick's district, Shapiro is predicted to coast to victory by double digits, Covey said.Pennsylvania also has three other neck-and-neck races that together could decide control of the House. Two Republican incumbents, Reps. Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th District and Scott Perry in the 10th, are seeking reelection in races labeled "Lean D." Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan, in Pennsylvania's 8th District, is in a "toss up" race, according to the Cook Report.Fitzpatrick, however, noted he won nearly 55% of voters in his district in 2022, even as Shapiro won 59% of the vote in the district, evidence to him that his constituents are more than willing to split their tickets.Independent public polling on the race for the district is sparse, though a recent internal survey conducted by Global Strategy Group for the Harvie campaign showed him and Fitzpatrick tied. A September poll conducted by Public Opinion Strategies for the National Republican Congressional Committee and Fitzpatrick's campaign had the incumbent up by 9 percentage points. A poll released Sunday by The New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University found Harvie with a narrow 48% to 46% lead over Fitzpatrick — within the poll's margin of error.Recent outside spending paints a competitive picture. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has committed more than $1.5 million to TV ads in the district since the start of October, while House Democrats' main super PAC has pitched in more than $7.5 million, according to AdImpact data. Before this election, neither group had bought TV ads in the district since 2020. Republicans are also shelling out to shore up Fitzpatrick. The House GOP's main super PAC, the Congressional Leadership Fund, and the NRCC have committed just under $5 million and just over $1 million, respectively, to ads in the district, according to AdImpact. And Trump's super PAC, MAGA Inc., recently purchased $100,000 in ads in the district opposing Harvie, according to an Oct. 12 Federal Election Commission filing."Here's how you know where his loyalties lie," Pennsylvania Democratic Party Chair Eugene DePasquale told CNBC. "Donald Trump and MAGA Inc. coming in to spend $100,000 to bail him out because they know when push comes to shove, he'll be loyal to them."Fitzpatrick has a significant cash advantage, with more than $709,000 in his war chest as of Oct. 14 according to FEC filings, compared with Harvie's just over $409,000 in cash on hand.Reilly Richardson, a spokesperson for the NRCC, pointed to this fundraising disparity, saying Harvie had "a stagnant campaign" and "a significant cash disadvantage."

schema.headline: Can GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a moderate who's bucked Trump, keep his Pennsylvania swing seat?

title: Lula wins Brazil runoff after prediction markets favored Bolsonaro
description: Brazil's President and presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva waves a national flag during a campaign rally in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on Sept. 2
body: Brazil's President and presidential candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva waves a national flag during a campaign rally in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on Sept. 26, 2026. Miguel Schincariol | Afp | Getty ImagesLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva was reelected president of Brazil on Sunday in a runoff election, an upset that prediction markets odds failed to anticipate.Lula defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing candidate and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, by 51.8% to 48.2%, according to the country's Superior Electoral Court. As late as Sunday afternoon, Lula remained a significant underdog on prediction markets. Even just after 8:30 p.m. ET on Sunday, Lula's odds were at 21% on Kalshi. Bolsonaro's odds on prediction markets surged after first-round voting on Oct. 4, with both Kalshi and Polymarket giving Bolsonaro an over 80% chance of ousting Lula. The Kalshi contract asked, "Brazil Presidential election winner?" and was verified by reporting from the Associated Press. Kalshi co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour has previously defended Kalshi's election contracts. In August, Kalshi reflected a 95% likelihood of Wisconsin Democratic socialist Francesca Hong winning the Democratic gubernatorial primary over Milwaukee County executive David Crowley. Instead, Hong lost the race by less than 1 percentage point. "Before the 'prediction markets got it wrong' headlines roll in: a 5% probability doesn't mean it won't happen," Mansour wrote in an Aug. 12 social media post on X. "It means it should happen 1 in 20 times. If 5% candidates never won, the markets would be broken."Odds and prediction market platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.Unlike prediction market odds, which pointed to a clear Bolsonaro victory, political polls showed a tight race in the days leading up to the contest.Brazil's Supreme Court also extended voting for two hours late Sunday, which Bolsonaro argued hurt his chances of winning the presidency. Bolsonaro is expected to challenge the outcome, Reuters reported. Following Lula's victory, Brazil-linked stocks and ETFs slid on Monday. The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) shed 22%, while U.S.-traded shares of Itau Unibanco and Banco Bradesco tanked 20% and nearly 30%, respectively. Brewer Ambev and Petrobras each declined more than 15%. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: Lula wins Brazil runoff after prediction markets favored Bolsonaro

title: Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) at the opening bell in New York City on October 19, 2026. Angela Weiss | Afp | Getty I
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) at the opening bell in New York City on October 19, 2026. Angela Weiss | Afp | Getty ImagesA version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading. Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up. Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova,  Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff. Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies. AI trade loses steamThe ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week. Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF  are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.  Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24. Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year. Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500. Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.  Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors. Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

schema.headline: Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

title: Trump says he'll soon decide whether to ‘make a deal’ with Iran or ‘finish it off'
description: US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before boarding Marine One as he departs the White House for Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, en route to F
body: US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before boarding Marine One as he departs the White House for Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, en route to Fort Myers, Florida, on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, DC, US, October 23, 2026.Evan Vucci | ReutersU.S. President Donald Trump has said he was deciding whether to "make a deal" with Iran or "finish it off" as investors weigh heightened tensions across the Middle East."Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? It's getting to be decision time," Trump said in a Fox News interview on Sunday.Mediators from Qatar, which has played a key role in efforts to negotiate an agreement between Washington and Tehran, visited Tehran on Sunday, according to Reuters. It comes as attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia continued over the weekend.The last confirmed U.S. strikes on Iran were on Sept. 1. Trump previously said attacks would not resume until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Tehran says it is preparing a military response to any U.S. strikes.A potential U.S. target could be Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried site linked to Iran's nuclear program, Trump said in the Sunday interview."We can read the badge on somebody's shirt from space, okay? We know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe Mountain. We know the other three [nuclear sites] are obliterated," Trump said.Trump also repeated the claim that the U.S. controls the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for global trade and a major flashpoint in the conflict, citing that crude oil flows have returned to prewar levels.Energy prices nonetheless remain elevated amid the disruption and a global refining squeeze.Washington and Tehran have both repeatedly claimed they control the route, where overall trade flows remain severely curtailed, impacting consumer prices.A Singapore-flagged container ship sank in the strait earlier this month after being struck by an unidentified projectile and catching fire.Ali Ozmaei, chief of the Iran Revolutionary Guard navy, said earlier this month that Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships.Regional powers seek Iran talksSenior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are meeting Iran's leadership in Tehran on MondayThe three countries signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in August, committing to closer defense cooperation and stipulating that an armed attack against one member would be regarded as an attack against all.It is the first meeting of the group since Houthi missiles and drones targeted sites across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh airport and an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco.Saudi Arabia last week postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference until 2027 due to security concerns after a string of fatal strikes.

title: Elon Musk says more than 200 neoclouds face 'guppy-level death'
description: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a press briefing held by President Donald Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outsid
body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a press briefing held by President Donald Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026.Finn Gomez | Getty ImagesElon Musk said that more than 200 neocloud companies could collapse, sending shares in those companies whipsawing.Nebius, Iren and CoreWeave all fell in early trading, adding pressure to a sector already facing investor concerns about debt-fueled expansion and whether the large AI infrastructure buildout will generate returns. The stocks all rebounded later in the day."As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers," Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, said on a post on X on Sunday."That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many," he added.Musk's SpaceX operates its own data centers through which it sells computing capacity. SpaceX is a direct competitor to the neoclouds which also rent compute. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoreWeave, Nebius and Iren shares over the past five days.Musk was replying to a post on X by Chamath Palihapitiya, the founder of Social Capital, who laid out his views on the state of the data center buildout. He suggested that there will be "a lot of partially stranded compute and compute sitting in inventory in 2027 than is currently forecasted," which will be "bought and paid for but effectively underearning (below total cost of capital) or collecting dust.""2027 will be a turbulent year because it will clear out a bunch of wrong/bad bets. It will also be a consolidation year for a few," Palihapitiya said.Neocloud stocks have taken a hammering over the past month, with CoreWeave and Nebius down more than 30% while Iren has tanked 40%. The sell-off started earlier this month after the spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps hit levels generally viewed as signs of distress. The yields on CoreWeave's bonds also climbed. Investors have grown jittery over companies that are borrowing heavily to fund the purchase of expensive Nvidia chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power. watch nowNvidia, neoclouds defend demandNvidia, an investor in several neoclouds, looked to shore up the sector last week at its GTC event in Berlin, Germany. In an interview with CNBC, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the demand for neoclouds is "off the charts.""What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth… because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital," Huang said."The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital. That's going to get solved," he added.Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer at Nebius, distanced his company from concerns surrounding CoreWeave, saying "we're not carrying the kind of debt that they are," in an interview with CNBC. Boroditsky said that if the AI infrastructure company brought its 2027 capacity online, it would sell out. And there could be "the same type of dynamic" in 2028.watch nowIren Co-CEO Daniel Roberts also defended demand."We understand the increased focus from investors, but when we're talking from customers, nothing has changed. The demand is still there," Roberts told CNBC last week. "Next year, we are having conversations with customers covering multiples of all the capacity we possibly bring online, and in the last month or so, 2028 is now coming into focus. But the demand is there," he added.

schema.headline: Elon Musk says more than 200 neoclouds face 'guppy-level death'

title: Audi defends plans for a $4 billion Georgia plant amid VW restructuring, tariffs
description: The Audi logo can be seen on a car dealership in Manhattan. Picture Alliance | Picture Alliance | Getty ImagesDETROIT — Audi's CEO defended the carmak
body: The Audi logo can be seen on a car dealership in Manhattan. Picture Alliance | Picture Alliance | Getty ImagesDETROIT — Audi's CEO defended the carmaker's plans for a new $4 billion plant in Georgia on Sunday, calling it a business decision aimed at growing sales and reducing exposure to U.S. tariffs.The plant, set to be Audi's first in the U.S., was announced Saturday by President Donald Trump during a rally in Georgia, near where the Volkswagen-owned luxury brand plans to build the new SUV-producing facility."We have significantly greater ambitions for Audi in America," Audi CEO Gernot Dollner said during a media roundtable Sunday. "The United States is the second largest premium market in the world, and today we are not fully exploiting this potential. We are changing that."The announcement comes amid an intense restructuring of its VW parent company, including plans to cut 50,000 jobs and close four German plants, including an Audi facility, between 2031 and ​2034.Dollner, who joined Trump at the rally, said the decision for a plant in the U.S. was years in the making, with more than 70 locations evaluated over "many months" and "intense" negotiations with public officials."This is not a decision against Germany. Germany remains the backbone of Audi," Dollner said. "We develop our cars here. Our technologies are created here, and Georgia does not take any task away from us in Germany."watch nowDollner said localized production is the best decision for the brand, which has struggled in sales this decade amid rising operational costs and Trump's tariffs on vehicles from Germany and other countries into the U.S. Current tariffs on vehicles from Germany are 15%, down from 25%.Last year, U.S. tariffs cost Audi 1.2 billion euros ($1.4 billion), as it imports all its vehicles for the U.S. market from Europe or Mexico.Dollner said the Trump administration asked Audi to announce the new plant at the Georgia rally promoting Republicans ahead of Nov. 3 midterm elections."It was … a three-year project that, at the end, by coincidence, led to that moment yesterday," he said Sunday. "With respect of the office and country, we joined the invitation."Dollner noted Audi is the last major German luxury brand to establish U.S. production after Mercedes-Benz and BMW.The company said the Georgia plant is expected to begin production of Audi's Q7, Q8 and Q9 in the early 2030s. The plant would have the capacity to produce up to 200,000 vehicles annually, roughly half of which the automaker said will be exported outside the U.S."This is to make Audi obviously a significant player here in the U.S. market," said Audi of America President Vito Paladino during the roundtable. He also said additional details on U.S. investments and production are forthcoming.Audi's U.S. deliveries were roughly flat through the third quarter of this year, following a 16% decline from 2024 to 2025.

schema.headline: Audi defends plans for a $4 billion Georgia plant amid VW restructuring, tariffs

title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push
description: watch nowMicrosoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infra
body: watch nowMicrosoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.The software maker announced a new voluntary exit offer for certain workers in the U.S., Canada, India and the United Kingdom at its experience level of 70 or below. Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter. The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people.Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies. That put a strain on Microsoft's finances. In April, it announced a first-ever voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for. Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees."The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees. "This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program."Microsoft is in the midst of a business model transformation, increasingly trying to charge clients based on how much AI they actually use. It has armed programmers, sellers and supply chain workers with AI tools and observed noticeable results. At the same time, the 51-year-old maker of Windows and Office wants to ensure that it has the right talent to go after its most compelling new growth opportunities.The idea is to make the shift without weakening Microsoft's financial profile. In the second quarter, cloud rivals Alphabet and Amazon both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed $19.64 billion in positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year.Some marketing, sales and engineering teams have decided not to participate in the new buyout, the person said. Employees must decide whether to take the offer in early December, and those participating will leave on Dec. 31, the person added.More than 30% of those who could join the voluntary retirement program went ahead with it, Microsoft said in July. But that was open to those at the senior director level and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan. The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around.On Wednesday, Microsoft is scheduled to report third-quarter results.WATCH: Amazon, Microsoft earnings key to gauging AI investment returns: CIOwatch now

schema.headline: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push

title: Meta announces $95 billion stock offering to fund AI expansion
description: Meta said Monday it is planning to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure and superintellig
body: Meta said Monday it is planning to raise a total of $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure and superintelligence.The stock was down 1.6% in morning trading after the announcement. Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares, Meta said in a statement.The tech giant will initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.The news comes as hyperscalers pour record sums into the AI infrastructure build-out. Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related capital spending could total about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031, across compute, data centers and power.Meta's planned investments will support "emerging AI opportunities" including its family of apps, its AI agent Muse and its data center business, the company said Monday.It plans to balance funding for these investments through a mix of operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, partnerships and equity capital.Meta racing to secure AI infrastructureMeta is among the major hyperscalers that are increasingly tapping debt to fund the expensive infrastructure required for the AI boom.Last week, Meta posted third-quarter results showing revenue jumped 26% year on year: $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. However, investors focused more on the tech company's negative free cash flow and its higher full-year capital expenditure forecast.It now expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from $130 billion. That sent Meta's shares lower on Thursday. Meta is building four "superclusters" with more than 1 gigawatt of capacity each and is on track to nearly double total infrastructure capacity in 2026 on a year-over-year basis, the company said.The decision to raise more money "reflects the eye-watering levels of investment required to keep up in the AI arms race," Ben Wood, senior partner at CCS Insight, told CNBC. "Meta offering more stock comes at a time when numerous companies, such as Google, SpaceX and soon, Anthropic, are going to the markets to raise funds."Alphabet, Google's parent company, said it would look to raise $85 billion in June. SpaceX has closed a $40 billion debt financing to purchase graphics processing units. Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering.TikTok U.S. is looking to secure multiple gigawatts of computing capacity over the coming years, CNBC reported Friday.

schema.headline: Meta announces $95 billion stock offering to fund AI expansion

title: Brazilian stocks rocked as Lula wins presidential election, Bolsonaro reportedly refuses to concede
description: SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - OCTOBER 24: Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva, incumbent president of Brazil and presidential candidate for Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT)
body: SAO PAULO, BRAZIL - OCTOBER 24: Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva, incumbent president of Brazil and presidential candidate for Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT) waves a Brazil flag during a rally ahead of the presidential runoff at Avenida Paulista on October 24, 2026 in Sao Paulo, Brazil.  Alexandre Schneider | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won an unprecedented fourth term as Brazil's president, overturning a first-round loss to beat Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. The outcome triggered a sell-off in Brazilian assets as markets were caught off guard.Lula took 51.8% of valid votes to Bolsonaro's 48.2%, according to the Superior Electoral Court, with nearly all ballots counted on Sunday.The results are also historic as it's the first time since Brazil returned to direct elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the final runoff after losing in the first round.Markets jolted by Lula win Brazilian stocks plunged following the unexpected victory, unwinding some of the rally from the first-round result three weeks earlier. That reflected expectations of more market-friendly policymaking by Bolsonaro and broader jitters around Brazil's debt and spending.The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF was 25% lower at 10:30 a.m. ET, while trading on Brazil's stock exchange was halted by an automatic circuit breaker. U.S.-listed Brazilian companies also sold off. Energy giant Petrobras was last seen down 16%, banking group Itaú Unibanco fell 20%, brewer Ambev shed 10.3%, and mining firm Vale fell 1.2%. Aircraft manufacturer Embraer was 5% lower.The Brazilian real meanwhile dropped 10.5% against the U.S. dollar to its lowest level since December 2025, according to LSEG data. The Brazilian Treasury on Monday canceled auctions of inflation-linked and fixed-rate government bonds that had been scheduled for Oct. 27 and Oct. 29, saying in a notice that it would "continue to monitor market conditions and act to ensure the proper functioning of the government bond market and other related assets." An auction of Treasury Financial Bills scheduled for Oct. 27 will go ahead.Citi analysts said Monday that investors were concerned about "fiscal policy, state-owned enterprises, and the broader reform agenda" under Lula, who began his current term on Jan. 1, 2023. He was previously Brazil's president from 2003 to 2011. Banking stocks will be hit by the risk that interest rates remain higher for longer, delaying the normalization of banks' asset quality, Citi analysts also said.watch nowLula's leadership has seen mounting public debt driven by double-digit interest rates, elevated costs of servicing the debt, and rigid mandatory spending. He has pledged to extend the Bolsa Família social welfare system and reduce the working week without pay cuts."The fiscal side has always been Brazil's Achilles heel, and a 7-8% budget deficit and 70% net debt-to-GDP ratio leave Brazil vulnerable in a global bond sell-off," Chris Turner, ING's head of EMEA and Latam research, said in a note."Instead of fiscal consolidation under Bolsonaro, Brazilian assets are instead going to have to contend with Lula's campaign pledges, including a shorter working week," Turner said.Alejo Czerwonko, a fellow at the Atlantic Council, said Lula's administration will likely extend the more "gradual approach" to stabilizing its debt trajectory, building on the existing fiscal framework while seeking to preserve public investment and social spending.Goldman Sachs analysts said they expect "modest measures" to contain the government's spending growth, alongside further increases in an already high tax burden, while major structural reforms remain unlikely. Vote tensionsFinancial markets will also be monitoring how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result or "allows the constitution to run its course," ING's Turner added.Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat overnight, saying he would seek to have the result annulled, Reuters reported. He also said a ruling by a supreme court justice to extend voting for two hours was "unacceptable," according to the outlet.The election process was marred by allegations of voter suppression, with Lula's campaign reporting suspended public transportation in some key areas. Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin extended voting by two hours. Bolsonaro's campaign had also requested an extension, citing heavy rains that shut polling stations in the south, a right-wing stronghold.  Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazilian presidential candidate, speaks during a press conference at the Liberal Party (PL) camp following the runoff election in Brasilia, Brazil, on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026.  Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe victory of the 80-year-old leftist, who had trailed in the first round, blocks a rightward shift in Latin America that U.S. President Donald Trump has backed. Trump called Bolsonaro's lead in the first round "a very, very big victory."He would have preferred a Brazilian president in closer alignment to U.S. foreign policy as Washington makes efforts to project U.S. power across the Americas, according to Daniela Portella Sampaio, senior research fellow for Latin American Security at the U.K. think tank Royal United Services Institute. Lula, who has publicly sparred with Trump, is set to govern from 2027 to 2030, facing a Congress where Bolsonaro's Liberal Party holds the largest bench in decades, and with a substantial public debt that he would need to stabilize. Leaders from across Latin America largely congratulated Lula's historic win. Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori hailed Lula's victory in a post on X late Sunday, calling it a "democratic day" for the Brazilian people. Uruguay President Yamandú Orsi congratulated Lula over a call, calling the Brazilian president a "friend."— CNBC's Matthew Tan contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Brazilian stocks rocked as Lula wins presidential election, Bolsonaro reportedly refuses to concede
